story.title: The Handpump
paragraphs_en: Once upon a time, many years ago, in a town was a hand pump. The town was a small one, disconnected from the rest of the world. It was filled with dust during the day and on winter mornings, it was wrapped in mist. Usually it was very quiet, the only faint sounds that one could hear were the chirping of birds and the moving of bullock carts. In the same town, there was a huge mansion. In it, an old woman lived all alone. All her family members had died. She did not like speaking to people. She had a hand pump through which she used to draw water. This made things easy for her as it was not comfortable for her to go far away to the well or the little stream that was situated just outside of town. Then, one spring she noticed that the flow of the water from the handpump had reduced considerably.

By summer, the handpump ran dry. Not even a drop of water came out of it. The old lady wondered what had gone wrong. Soon, all the water stored in the house in pots would get exhausted. What was she to do? She couldn’t use her hand pump now. She asked the vegetable seller who passed by her house about the water shortage. He informed her that not only her mansion, but the entire lane, the entire town and actually the entire district was suffering from the same problem. The townspeople had used so much groundwater that the water levels had fallen drastically. Now, their wells, tanks and hand pumps were all dry. “What will we do now?” said the worried vegetable seller. “We should have thought about this earlier when we were recklessly drawing water from those huge borewells for our factories and agriculture. But there is no use crying over spilled milk,“ the old lady said and sighed. “Something needs to be done urgently. We must revive our groundwater tables,” she said firmly. But they both knew that the path wouldn’t be easy.

Earlier, the old lady did not speak much to people but she knew that if she had to stand up for a cause, then connecting to people would be the key. She especially gathered all the town’s ladies and they organized meetings every Thursday at some or the other person’s house. Not only did they discuss something constructive, but they also formed a strong social circuit. Slowly, the children and later the townsmen joined too. By the time rains were due, almost the entire town used to be at these meetings. The town hall that was locked up a few years ago because everyone was busy chatting on the internet, was now reopened. “We have closed all the major borewells, and most of the water that we take is from the little stream outside the town. But I still don’t understand why the water tables are not rising,” said Sheetal, a young sixteen year old. “Sheetal, groundwater is not replenished overnight. It will take some time, maybe a few years,“ said the village sarpanch.

“Monsoon is just about to begin. I am sure that when the rains come, everything will get sorted out,” said the old lady. “I think we are going in the wrong direction. We are not focusing on what we should,” said Navin. Navin was a primary school teacher at the Government Town School. He taught Geography and knew a great deal about plants, animals, rivers, mountains and land. “What do you mean that we are not focusing on what we should?” asked the old lady politely. Navin said, “I feel that we are not taking the right steps. Even if the rains come, it will do little good in reviving the groundwater. Our main problem is concrete. Concrete does not absorb rainwater the way earth does. Most water runs off from the surface of the concrete or gets evaporated. This is the biggest way water is wasted and the reason why water tables do not revive.”

The people of the town understood the point he was trying to make. They decided that they must increase more open spaces in the town, free from concrete and cement so that water could seep back to the soil. Under the guidance of Navin, the village took several steps in this direction. The spaces that were littered with plastic bags and tins were cleaned and open spaces were created. The concrete pavements outside the homes and shops were broken down and land was exposed. The Panchayat prohibited the construction of any concrete building for the next two years, till the time the groundwater hadn’t revived. Fresh tanks were installed and the old ones were cleaned to store water when it rained.

Once enough water was stored, it was thrown onto a dry patch of land. The parched and thirsty earth absorbed the water very quickly, giving a moist fragrance. And guess what, four months after the rains were over and these methods implemented, the old lady decided to use her hand pump again. At first, there was a trickle, then the water came out in full intensity, it was sweet, fresh and crystal clear. The same was the case with the whole lane, the town and the entire district. The groundwater was finally revived! The town people were now in a closely-knit social circuit and happier than ever before!

“Sheetal, groundwater is not replenished overnight.
It will take some time, maybe a few years,“ said the village sarpanch.
“Monsoon is just about to begin.
I am sure that when the rains come, everything will get sorted out,” said the old lady.
“I think we are going in the wrong direction.
We are not focusing on what we should,” said Navin.
Navin was a primary school teacher at the Government Town School.
He taught Geography and knew a great deal about plants, animals, rivers, mountains and land.
“What do you mean that we are not focusing on what we should?” asked the old lady politely.
Navin said, “I feel that we are not taking the right steps.
Even if the rains come, it will do little good in reviving the groundwater.
Our main problem is concrete.
Concrete does not absorb rainwater the way earth does.
Most water runs off from the surface of the concrete or gets evaporated.
This is the biggest way water is wasted and the reason why water tables do not revive.”
The people of the town understood the point he was trying to make.
They decided that they must increase more open spaces in the town, free from concrete and cement so that water could seep back to the soil.
Under the guidance of Navin, the village took several steps in this direction.
The spaces that were littered with plastic bags and tins were cleaned and open spaces were created.
The concrete pavements outside the homes and shops were broken down and land was exposed.
The Panchayat prohibited the construction of any concrete building for the next two years, till the time the groundwater hadn’t revived.
Fresh tanks were installed and the old ones were cleaned to store water when it rained.
Once enough water was stored, it was thrown onto a dry patch of land.
The parched and thirsty earth absorbed the water very quickly, giving a moist fragrance.
And guess what, four months after the rains were over and these methods implemented, the old lady decided to use her hand pump again.
At first, there was a trickle, then the water came out in full intensity, it was sweet, fresh and crystal clear.
The same was the case with the whole lane, the town and the entire district.
The groundwater was finally revived!
The town people were now in a closely-knit social circuit and happier than ever before!
